arXiv:2503.16296v2 [math.AG] 04 Apr 2025

Log-Concavity of the Grothendieck Classes of Banana Graphs and Clasped Necklaces

Stephanie Chen Address: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 02138, U.S.A. Email address: stephchen@math.harvard.edu
Abstract.

The Grothendieck classes of melonic graphs satisfy a recursive relation and may be written as polynomials in the class of the moduli space ℳ0,4\mathcal{M}_{0,4} with nonnegative integer coefficients, conjectured to be log-concave. In this article, we investigate log-concavity and ultra-log-concavity for the Grothendieck class of banana graphs and the three families of polynomials involved in the recursive relation. We prove that all four are log-concave, establishing the specific case of banana graphs for the log-concavity conjecture. We additionally introduce the infinite family of clasped necklaces, melonic graphs obtained by replacing an edge of a 22-banana with a string of mm-bananas. Using the recursive relation, we explicitly compute the classes of clasped necklaces and prove that they too are log-concave.

1. Introduction

In a series of papers beginning with [AM09], Aluffi and Marcolli study the algebro-geometric Feynman rule defined by associating to a Feynman graph Γ\Gamma the class of its graph hypersurface complement 𝕌⁡(Γ)\mathbb{U}(\Gamma) in the Grothendieck ring of varieties. Aluffi, Marcolli, and Qaisar apply this process to melonic graphs in [AMQ23], motivated by the appearance of melonic graphs as the dominating diagrams in the large NN limit for the O​(N)3O(N)^{3} tensor model of Klebanov and Tarnopolsky [KT17]. After obtaining a recursive formula for computing the Grothendieck classes of melonic graphs, they proved that the classes may be written as polynomials in the class 𝕊:=[ℳ0,4]\mathbb{S}:=[\mathcal{M}_{0,4}] with positive integer coefficients and further conjectured that these polynomials are log-concave, i.e. the coefficients satisfy the inequality ai−1​ai+1≤ai2a_{i-1}a_{i+1}\leq a_{i}^{2}.

In this note, we prove the conjecture for two infinite families of melonic graphs and further investigate log-concavity and related properties of the polynomials which appear in the recursive formula.

1.1. Banana graphs

In scalar field theory, one studies the Feynman graphs of the theory; these are finite graphs with both internal edges (edges which have both a starting and ending vertex) and external ‘half edges’ (only one end attached to a vertex) that satisfy certain properties in relation to the Langrangian for the theory. To each Feynman graph of a given theory we associate a Feynman integral which captures the combinatorics of the graph. In sufficiently large spacetime dimension, the integral is defined on the complement of the vanishing locus of the Kirchhoff-Symanzik polynomial of the graph ΨΓ​(t)\Psi_{\Gamma}(t), a homogeneous polynomial in the internal edges of the graph. Consequently, in [AM11a], Aluffi and Marcolli define the Grothendieck class of a graph with nn internal edges to be the class [𝔸n∖X^Γ][\mathbb{A}^{n}\setminus\hat{X}_{\Gamma}] in the Grothendieck ring of varieties K0​(Varℚ)K_{0}(\text{Var}_{\mathbb{Q}}), where X^Γ\hat{X}_{\Gamma} is the vanishing locus of ΨΓ​(t)\Psi_{\Gamma}(t) in 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}. This process is described briefly in section 2.2 below and in far more detail in [Mar10a] and [Mar10b].

Banana graphs are graphs consisting of two vertices and multiple edges between them. An nn-banana, denoted Γn\Gamma_{n}, is a banana graph with nn edges. The physical motivation behind studying banana graphs comes from scalar field theories with an interaction term of the form ℒint​(ϕ)=ϕn\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}}(\phi)=\phi^{n}, for which Γn\Gamma_{n} is a vacuum bubble Feynman graph, i.e. a Feynman graph without external edges. The associated Feynman integral takes the form (cf. [AM09, Lem 1.8])

(1.1) U⁡(Γn,p)=Γ⁡((1−D2)​(n−1)+1)​C​(p)(4​π)(n−1)​D2​∫σn(t1​…​tn)(D2−1)​(n−1)−1​ωnΨΓ​(t)(D2−1)​nU(\Gamma_{n},p)=\frac{\Gamma((1-\frac{D}{2})(n-1)+1)C(p)}{(4\pi)^{\frac{(n-1)D}{2}}}\int_{\sigma_{n}}\frac{(t_{1}\ldots t_{n})^{(\frac{D}{2}-1)(n-1)-1}\omega_{n}}{\Psi_{\Gamma}(t)^{(\frac{D}{2}-1)n}}

where

C⁡(p)=(∑v∈V⁡(Γ)∑e∈Eext​(Γn),t⁡(e)=vpe)2C(p)=(\sum_{v\in V(\Gamma)}\sum_{e\in E_{\text{ext}}(\Gamma_{n}),t(e)=v}p_{e})^{2}

is a function of the external momentum, DD is the spacetime dimension for the theory, σn\sigma_{n} is the simplex

σn={(t1,…,tn)∈ℝ+n|∑iti=1},\sigma_{n}=\{(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}|\sum_{i}t_{i}=1\},

ωn\omega_{n} is the volume form, and

ΨΓn​(t)=∑i=1n∏j≠itj\Psi_{\Gamma_{n}}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j\neq i}t_{j}

is the Kirchhoff-Symanzik polynomial for Γn\Gamma_{n}. In [AM09], the authors use the Cremona transformation to compute the Grothendieck class of banana graphs, obtaining the formula

(1.2) 𝔹n:=[𝔸n∖X^Γn]=𝕋​𝕋n−(−1)n𝕋+1+n​𝕋n−1\mathbb{B}_{n}:=[\mathbb{A}^{n}\setminus\hat{X}_{\Gamma_{n}}]=\mathbb{T}\frac{\mathbb{T}^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{T}+1}+n\mathbb{T}^{n-1}

where 𝕋:=[𝔾m]\mathbb{T}:=[\mathbb{G}_{m}] is the Grothendieck class of the multiplicative group.

This paper focuses more generally on melonic graphs, discussed in detail in [AMQ23]. Melonic graphs are constructed by iteratively replacing edges with a string of banana graphs. Using the deletion-contraction relation for the Grothendieck class of a graph derived in [AM11b], the authors of [AMQ23] obtained a recursive formula for the Grothendieck class of melonic graphs in terms of the classes 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n} and the polynomials

(1.3) fn=𝕋n−(−1)n𝕋+1gn=n​𝕋n−1−𝕋n−(−1)n𝕋+1hn=𝕋n+(−1)n​𝕋𝕋+1.f_{n}=\frac{\mathbb{T}^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{T}+1}\quad\quad g_{n}=n\mathbb{T}^{n-1}-\frac{\mathbb{T}^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{T}+1}\quad\quad h_{n}=\frac{\mathbb{T}^{n}+(-1)^{n}\mathbb{T}}{\mathbb{T}+1}.

Using this recursive formula, they proved that the Grothendieck class of a melonic graph may be written as a polynomial in 𝕊=𝕋−1\mathbb{S}=\mathbb{T}-1 with nonnegative integer coefficients and conjectured that these polynomials are log-concave.

1.2. Log-concavity

A sequence a0,…,ana_{0},\ldots,a_{n} of real numbers is log-concave if it satisfies the property ak2≥ak−1​ak+1a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k-1}a_{k+1} for all 0<k<n0<k<n. One classical example of a log-concave sequence is given by the binomial sequence (n0),(n1),…,(nn){n\choose 0},{n\choose 1},\ldots,{n\choose n}. A real polynomial f⁡(x)=an​xn+…+a0f(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+\ldots+a_{0} is said to be log-concave if its coefficients a0,…,ana_{0},\ldots,a_{n} form a log-concave sequence. By a result of Newton’s, any real-rooted polynomial is log-concave [Sta06, Thm 2], [Brä14, Lem 1.1].

Log-concavity has been a central property of many conjectures, one of the most famous being the Heron-Rota-Welsh conjecture, which states the the characteristic polynomial of a matroid is log-concave. This conjecture was settled positively by Adiprasito, Huh, and Katz in [AHK18] using a combinatorial analogue of the Hodge-Riemann relations by studying the Chow ring of a matroid. A brief discussion of the proof is given in [Bak18]. See [Sta06], [Bre94], [Brä14] for more general surveys on log-concavity, related properties, and methods to prove sequences have these properties.

One of the main results we obtain in this paper is the following log-concavity result (cf. Theorem 3.4).

Theorem 1.1.

For all n≥0n\geq 0, the Grothendieck classes

(1.4) {𝔹n=(𝕊+1)​(𝕊+1)n−(−1)n𝕊+2+n​(𝕊+1)n−1fn​(𝕊)=(𝕊+1)n−(−1)n𝕊+2gn​(𝕊)=n​(𝕊+1)n−1−(𝕊+1)n−(−1)n𝕊+2hn​(𝕊)=(𝕊+1)n+(−1)n​(𝕊+1)𝕊+2\begin{cases}\mathbb{B}_{n}=(\mathbb{S}+1)\frac{(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{S}+2}+n(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n-1}\\ f_{n}(\mathbb{S})=\frac{(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{S}+2}\\ g_{n}(\mathbb{S})=n(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n-1}-\frac{(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{S}+2}\\ h_{n}(\mathbb{S})=\frac{(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n}+(-1)^{n}(\mathbb{S}+1)}{\mathbb{S}+2}\end{cases}

are all log-concave as polynomials in 𝕊\mathbb{S}.

In particular, this proves Conjecture 3.4 of [AMQ23] for all banana graphs. As a follow-up to this result, we consider the property of being ultra-log-concave, i.e. that the sequence (ak)(nk)\frac{(a_{k})}{{n\choose k}} is a log-concave sequence. We fully establish for which n≥1n\geq 1 the four polynomials 𝔹n,fn​(𝕊),gn​(𝕊),hn​(𝕊)\mathbb{B}_{n},f_{n}(\mathbb{S}),g_{n}(\mathbb{S}),h_{n}(\mathbb{S}) are respectively ultra-log-concave (cf. Proposition 3.8):

Proposition 1.2.

Let n≥4n\geq 4. If nn is odd, then 𝔹n,fn​(𝕊),gn​(𝕊),hn​(𝕊)\mathbb{B}_{n},f_{n}(\mathbb{S}),g_{n}(\mathbb{S}),h_{n}(\mathbb{S}) are all not ultra-log-concave as polynomials in 𝕊\mathbb{S}. If nn is even, only 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n} is ultra-log-concave.

We also establish log-concavity for another family of melonic graphs, denoted Gm,n′G^{\prime}_{m,n} for m≥1,n≥2m\geq 1,n\geq 2, called clasped necklaces. These are melonic graphs obtained from a 22-banana by replacing a single edge with a string of n−1n-1 mm-bananas. The clasped necklace G3,7′G^{\prime}_{3,7} is drawn below. Using the recursive formula, we obtain closed forms for the Grothendieck class of a clasped necklace (cf. Lemma 4.1) and further prove that they are all log-concave as polynomials in 𝕊\mathbb{S} (cf. Proposition 4.2).

1.3. Summary of paper

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we recall the recursive formula for the Grothendieck class of a melonic graph and some key results on log-concave polynomials that we use in our proofs. We present results on the log-concavity and ultra log-concavity of the polynomials (1.4) in section 3. For clarity, most of the computations used in the proofs are deferred until section 5. Finally, in section 4, we derive the Grothendieck classes of clasped necklaces and establish their log-concavity as polynomials in 𝕊\mathbb{S}.

2. Grothendieck classes of melonic graphs

2.1. Grothendieck ring of varieties

We first briefly recall the construction of the Grothendieck ring of varieties. Fix a field kk of characteristic 0. The Grothendieck group of kk-varieties, denoted K0​(Vark)K_{0}(\text{Var}_{k}), is the abelian group generated by isomorphism classes of kk-varieties modulo the cut-and-paste relation

[X]=[Y]+[X∖Y][X]=[Y]+[X\setminus Y]

for any variety XX and closed subvariety YY. The group K0​(Vark)K_{0}(\text{Var}_{k}) admits a ring structure by defining multiplication of classes of varieties by [X]⋅[Y]=[X×Y][X]\cdot[Y]=[X\times Y] and extending by linearity. The resulting ring is called the Grothendieck ring of kk-varieties. One may observe that any ring-valued invariant of algebraic kk-varieties which is preserved by isomorphisms, satisfies the cut-and-paste relation, and is multiplicative over products must factor through K0​(Vark)K_{0}(\text{Var}_{k}), hence the assignment of a variety XX to its Grothendieck class [X]∈K0​(Vark)[X]\in K_{0}(\text{Var}_{k}) may be viewed as a ‘universal Euler characteristic’.

We fix notation for a couple key classes. First, we denote by 𝕃:=[𝔸1]\mathbb{L}:=[\mathbb{A}^{1}] the class of the affine line. We also define 𝕋:=[𝔾m]=𝕃−1\mathbb{T}:=[\mathbb{G}_{m}]=\mathbb{L}-1 and 𝕊:=[ℙ1∖{0,1,∞}]=𝕋−1\mathbb{S}:=[\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}]=\mathbb{T}-1, the classes of the multiplicative group and the projective line with three points removed respectively. Note that 𝕊\mathbb{S} also arises as the class [ℳ0,4][\mathcal{M}_{0,4}] of the moduli space of stable genus 00 curves with 44 marked points.

2.2. Grothendieck class of a graph

In [AM11a], Aluffi and Marcolli describe a procedure for constructing algebro-geometric Feynman rules, which assign to each Feynman graph an invariant in a commutative ring ℛ\mathcal{R} satisfying certain conditions [AM11a, Def 2.2]. They defined a motivic Feynman rule to be one that factors through K0​(Varℚ)K_{0}(\text{Var}_{\mathbb{Q}}) via the Grothendieck class of a graph, to be defined below.

The main motivation came from Feynman rules in pertubative scalar field theory, where one considers one-particle-irreducible (1PI) Feynman graphs: finite edge-connected graphs where each vertex has valance equal to the degree of one of the monomials in the Langrangian for the theory, and each edge is either an internal edge connecting two vertices or an external edge with only one vertex. Fix N:=#​Eext​(Γ),n:=#​Eint​(Γ)N:=\#E_{\text{ext}}(\Gamma),n:=\#E_{\text{int}}(\Gamma) as the number of external and internal edges respectively. Let D∈ℕD\in\mathbb{N} be the spacetime dimension for the theory. In the massless case, the Feynman rules dictate that we associate to Γ\Gamma a formal integral

(2.1) U⁡(Γ,p)=C​Γ⁡(n−D​ℓ2)(4​π)D​ℓ2​∫σnPΓ​(t,p)−n+D​ℓ2​ωnΨΓ​(t)−n+(ℓ+1)​D2U(\Gamma,p)=C\frac{\Gamma(n-\frac{D\ell}{2})}{(4\pi)^{\frac{D\ell}{2}}}\int_{\sigma_{n}}\frac{P_{\Gamma}(t,p)^{-n+\frac{D\ell}{2}}\omega_{n}}{\Psi_{\Gamma}(t)^{-n+(\ell+1)\frac{D}{2}}}

where C=∏v∈V⁡(Γ)λv​(2​π)DC=\prod_{v\in V(\Gamma)}\lambda_{v}(2\pi)^{D} with λv\lambda_{v} the coupling constant for the monomial of the Lagrangian with degree equal to the valence of vv, ωn\omega_{n} is the volume form of the simplex σn={t=(t1,…,tn)∈ℝ+n|∑iti=1}\sigma_{n}=\{t=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}|\sum_{i}t_{i}=1\}, ℓ:=b1​(Γ)\ell:=b_{1}(\Gamma) is the first Betti number of Γ\Gamma, and PΓ​(t,p),ΨΓ​(t)P_{\Gamma}(t,p),\Psi_{\Gamma}(t) are homogeneous polynomials in t1,…,tnt_{1},\ldots,t_{n} defined as follows.

Fix some ordering of the internal edges Eint​(Γ)={e1,…,en}E_{\text{int}}(\Gamma)=\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}\}. For each external edge e∈Eext​(Γ)e\in E_{\text{ext}}(\Gamma), let pep_{e} be the incoming external momentum associated to ee. For any cut-set CC dividing Γ\Gamma into two connected components Γ=Γ1∪Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{2}, we set

sC=(∑v∈V⁡(Γ1)Pv)2=(∑v∈V⁡(Γ2)Pv)2s_{C}=\left(\sum_{v\in V(\Gamma_{1})}P_{v}\right)^{2}=\left(\sum_{v\in V(\Gamma_{2})}P_{v}\right)^{2}

where

Pv=∑e∈Eext​(Γ),t⁡(e)=vpe.P_{v}=\sum_{e\in E_{\text{ext}}(\Gamma),t(e)=v}p_{e}.

The second Symanzik polynomial PΓ​(t,p)P_{\Gamma}(t,p) is then given by

(2.2) PΓ​(t,p)=∑C⊆ΓsC​∏ei∈CtiP_{\Gamma}(t,p)=\sum_{C\subseteq\Gamma}s_{C}\prod_{e_{i}\in C}t_{i}

where the sum is taken over all cut-sets of Γ\Gamma. This is a homogeneous polynomial of degree ℓ+1\ell+1.

The Kirchhoff-Symanzik polynomial ΨΓ​(t)\Psi_{\Gamma}(t) is defined by

(2.3) ΨΓ​(t)=∑T⊆Γ∏ei∉E⁡(T)ti\Psi_{\Gamma}(t)=\sum_{T\subseteq\Gamma}\prod_{e_{i}\notin E(T)}t_{i}

where the sum is taken over all spanning trees of Γ\Gamma. Note that ΨΓ​(t)\Psi_{\Gamma}(t), which is homogeneous of degree ℓ\ell, may be defined for any finite graph GG. The Kirchhoff-Symanzik polynomial may also be defined as the determinant of a ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell matrix MΓ​(t)M_{\Gamma}(t) associated to the graph; see section 1.2 of [AM09] for more details.

In the massive case, the parametric Feynman integral takes the form

(2.4) U⁡(Γ,p)=C​Γ⁡(n−D​ℓ2)(4​π)D​ℓ2​∫σnVΓ​(t,p)−n+D​ℓ2​ωnΨΓ​(t)D2U(\Gamma,p)=C\frac{\Gamma(n-\frac{D\ell}{2})}{(4\pi)^{\frac{D\ell}{2}}}\int_{\sigma_{n}}\frac{V_{\Gamma}(t,p)^{-n+\frac{D\ell}{2}}\omega_{n}}{\Psi_{\Gamma}(t)^{\frac{D}{2}}}

with the full formula for VΓ​(t,p)V_{\Gamma}(t,p) given by (3.15) in the proof of [Mar10b, Prop 3.1.7]. When D≥2​nℓD\geq\frac{2n}{\ell}, the integrals (2.1) and (2.4) are defined on the complement of the vanishing locus of ΨΓ​(t)\Psi_{\Gamma}(t). In the massless case, as the polynomials are homogeneous, we are interested in the complement in ℙn−1\mathbb{P}^{n-1} of the graph hypersurface

(2.5) XΓ={t∈ℙn−1|ΨΓ​(t)=0}.X_{\Gamma}=\{t\in\mathbb{P}^{n-1}|\Psi_{\Gamma}(t)=0\}.

In the massive case, we consider instead the complement in 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} of the affine hypersurface

(2.6) X^Γ={t∈𝔸n|ΨΓ​(t)=0}.\hat{X}_{\Gamma}=\{t\in\mathbb{A}^{n}|\Psi_{\Gamma}(t)=0\}.

In both settings, the assignment of U⁡(Γ,p)U(\Gamma,p) to Γ\Gamma satisfies a multiplicative property: if Γ\Gamma is a disjoint union Γ=Γ1∪Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{2}, then

U⁡(Γ,p)=U⁡(Γ1,p1)​U​(Γ2,p2).U(\Gamma,p)=U(\Gamma_{1},p_{1})U(\Gamma_{2},p_{2}).

To account for both the massless and massive cases, as well as preserve the multiplicative property (see [AM11a, Lem  2.3]), Aluffi and Marcolli defined a motivic Feynman rule to be an assignment of a Feynman graph Γ\Gamma to an invariant U⁡(Γ)∈ℛU(\Gamma)\in\mathcal{R} lying in a fixed commutative ring ℛ\mathcal{R} such that Γ↦U⁡(Γ)\Gamma\mapsto U(\Gamma) factors through a ring homomorphism K0​(Varℚ)→ℛK_{0}(\text{Var}_{\mathbb{Q}})\to\mathcal{R} via Γ↦[𝔸n∖X^Γ]\Gamma\mapsto[\mathbb{A}^{n}\setminus\hat{X}_{\Gamma}]. This leads us to the definition of the Grothendieck class of a finite graph in greater generality.

Definition 2.1.

Let GG be a finite graph. The Grothendieck class of GG is the class

(2.7) 𝕌⁡(G)=[𝔸n∖X^G]∈K0​(Varℚ)\mathbb{U}(G)=[\mathbb{A}^{n}\setminus\hat{X}_{G}]\in K_{0}(\text{Var}_{\mathbb{Q}})

with nn the number of edges of GG, and ΨG​(t),X^G\Psi_{G}(t),\hat{X}_{G} as defined in (2.3), (2.6).

Example 1 (Banana graphs).

A banana graph is a graph consisting of two vertices and multiple edges. We denote by 𝔹n\mathbb{B}_{n} the Grothendieck class of the banana graph with n>0n>0 edges. Then, (cf. [AM09, Thm 3.10], [AM11a, Lem 2.6], [AM11b, Cor 5.6])

(2.8) 𝔹n=𝕋​𝕋n−(−1)n𝕋+1+n​𝕋n−1=(𝕊+1)​(𝕊+1)n−(−1)n𝕊+2+n​(𝕊+1)n−1\mathbb{B}_{n}=\mathbb{T}\frac{\mathbb{T}^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{T}+1}+n\mathbb{T}^{n-1}=(\mathbb{S}+1)\frac{(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{S}+2}+n(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n-1}

In particular, letting LL be the 11-banana, we see that 𝕌⁡(L)=𝕃\mathbb{U}(L)=\mathbb{L}. Banana graphs and their Grothendieck classes are the focus of [AM09], in which lays much of the foundation for [AMQ23] due to the role of banana graphs as building blocks for melonic graphs.

The Grothendieck class of a graph satisfies the following properties with respect to elementary graph operations (cf. [AM11a, §2]):

  • •

    For two disjoint graphs Γ1,Γ2\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2} or two graphs that share only a single vertex,

    𝕌⁡(Γ1∪Γ2)=𝕌⁡(Γ1)​𝕌​(Γ2)\mathbb{U}(\Gamma_{1}\cup\Gamma_{2})=\mathbb{U}(\Gamma_{1})\mathbb{U}(\Gamma_{2})
  • •

    If Γ\Gamma is obtained by connecting two disjoint graphs Γ1,Γ2\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2} with a single edge, then

    𝕌⁡(Γ)=[𝔸1]​𝕌​(Γ1)​𝕌​(Γ2)\mathbb{U}(\Gamma)=[\mathbb{A}^{1}]\mathbb{U}(\Gamma_{1})\mathbb{U}(\Gamma_{2})
  • •

    If Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} is obtained from Γ\Gamma by attaching an edge to a vertex, then

    𝕌⁡(Γ′)=[𝔸1]​𝕌​(Γ)\mathbb{U}(\Gamma^{\prime})=[\mathbb{A}^{1}]\mathbb{U}(\Gamma)
  • •

    If Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} is obtained from Γ\Gamma by splitting an edge, then

    𝕌⁡(Γ′)=[𝔸1]​𝕌​(Γ)\mathbb{U}(\Gamma^{\prime})=[\mathbb{A}^{1}]\mathbb{U}(\Gamma)

Additionally in [AM11b], Aluffi and Marcolli derived a deletion-contraction relation for the Grothendieck classes of graphs. Let Γ\Gamma be a finite graph. Fix an edge ee in Γ\Gamma. We denote by Γ∖e\Gamma\setminus e the graph obtained from Γ\Gamma by deleting the edge ee and Γ/e\Gamma/e the graph obtained by contracting (i.e. identifying the two vertices of) the edge ee. Let Γn​e\Gamma_{ne} be the graph obtained by replacing ee by nn-multiple edges, i.e. an nn-banana for n>0n>0. In particular, Γe=Γ\Gamma_{e}=\Gamma and Γ0​e=Γ∖e\Gamma_{0e}=\Gamma\setminus e. We say that ee is a bridge if the removal of ee disconnects the graph and a looping edge if ee is attached to only one vertex. In the case that ee is neither a bridge nor a looping edge, we have the following deletion-contraction relation (cf. [AM11b, Thm 5.3])

(2.9) 𝕌⁡(Gn​e′)=fn​𝕌​(G′)+gn​𝕌​(G′/e)+hn​𝕌​(G′∖e)\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime}_{ne})=f_{n}\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime})+g_{n}\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime}/e)+h_{n}\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime}\setminus e)

where (cf. [AM11b, Cor 5.7])

(2.10) fn=𝕋n−(−1)n𝕋+1gn=n​𝕋n−1−𝕋n−(−1)n𝕋+1hn=𝕋n+(−1)n​𝕋𝕋+1f_{n}=\frac{\mathbb{T}^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{T}+1}\quad\quad g_{n}=n\mathbb{T}^{n-1}-\frac{\mathbb{T}^{n}-(-1)^{n}}{\mathbb{T}+1}\quad\quad h_{n}=\frac{\mathbb{T}^{n}+(-1)^{n}\mathbb{T}}{\mathbb{T}+1}

We note that notationally we have swapped gn,hng_{n},h_{n} in comparison to [AM11b] in order to match the notation used in [AMQ23]. These properties are useful for computing the Grothendieck class of a graph, as we demonstrate below.

2.3. Melonic graphs

The authors of [AMQ23] were interested in melonic graphs due to their role as the dominating diagram in the CTKT models of [BGRR11] in the large NN limit. Melonic graphs are graphs that may be constructed by starting with a single edge (and two vertices) and repeatedly replacing edges with strings of banana graphs. More precisely, a melonic construction is defined as follows.

Definition 2.2.

A nn-stage melonic construction is a list T=(t1,…,tn)T=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}) of tuples ts=(bs,ps,ks)t_{s}=(b_{s},p_{s},k_{s}) such that

  1. (1)

    bs=(a1,…,ars)b_{s}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{s}}) is a non-empty tuple of positive integers with length |bs|:=rs≥1|b_{s}|:=r_{s}\geq 1,

  2. (2)

    psp_{s} is an integer with p1=0p_{1}=0 and 0<ps<s0<p_{s}<s for s>1s>1,

  3. (3)

    ksk_{s} is an integer satisfying 1≤ks≤|bps|1\leq k_{s}\leq|b_{p_{s}}|,

  4. (4)

    and for all ti=((a1,…,ari),pi,ki)t_{i}=((a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{i}}),p_{i},k_{i}), i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, j=1,…,rij=1,\ldots,r_{i}, at most aja_{j} tuples ts=(bs,ps,ks)t_{s}=(b_{s},p_{s},k_{s}) are such that ps=i,ks=jp_{s}=i,k_{s}=j.

An nn-stage melonic construction is also said to have depth nn.

Each tuple in the melonic construction TT can be interpreted as a step in the corresponding melonic graph construction. One starts with a single edge connecting two vertices in stage 00. The first tuple t1=((a1,…,ar1),0,1)t_{1}=((a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{1}}),0,1) represents replacing the single edge of the first (and only) banana in stage 00 with a string of r1r_{1} bananas, where the iith banana has aia_{i} edges (1≤i≤r11\leq i\leq r_{1}). This is stage 11. Continuing, the tuple ts=((a1,…,ars),ps,ks)t_{s}=((a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{s}}),p_{s},k_{s}) corresponds to replacing a single edge of the ksk_{s}-th banana constructed in stage psp_{s} with a string of rsr_{s} bananas, again with the ii-th banana being an aia_{i}-banana (1≤i≤rs1\leq i\leq r_{s}). Stage pp is the resulting graph after applying pp tuples.

A melonic graph is a graph resulting from a melonic construction in this manner. As noted in [AMQ23], two different melonic constructions may determine the same melonic graph (up to graph isomorphism), in which case the constructions are said to be equivalent. If a melonic construction TT further satisfies the condition that for all ti=((a1,…,ari),pi,ki)t_{i}=((a_{1},\ldots,a_{r_{i}}),p_{i},k_{i}), i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, if aj=1a_{j}=1 then ks≠jk_{s}\neq j for all ss such that ps=ip_{s}=i, it is said to be reduced. In terms of the stage by stage construction, this is equivalent to no 11-banana constructed after stage 0 being replaced in a later stage. All melonic graphs admit a reduced construction ([AMQ23, Lem 2.1]).

The authors of [AMQ23] developed a recursive formula for calculating the Grothendieck class of a melonic graph, which we review here. Given a reduced melonic construction TT with a total of nn stages, the following cases are considered. First, if n=1n=1, i.e. TT corresponds to a graph that is a string of bananas t1=((a1,…,ar),0,1)t_{1}=((a_{1},\ldots,a_{r}),0,1), the Grothendieck class is simply a product of banana classes, 𝕌⁡(Γ)=∏i=1r𝔹ai\mathbb{U}(\Gamma)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb{B}_{a_{i}}. The second case is where n>1n>1 and tn=((a),p,k)t_{n}=((a),p,k) consists of adding a single aa-banana. An equivalent melonic construction of depth n−1n-1 may be obtained by omitting the last stage tnt_{n} and altering tpt_{p} such that the kkth banana added in stage pp has a−1a-1 extra edges than originally prescribed. In the third case, we consider a melonic construction of depth n>1n>1 such that tn=((1,…,1),p,k)t_{n}=((1,\ldots,1),p,k) corresponds to adding a string of rr 11-bananas. In terms of graph operations, this is equivalent to splitting an edge of the kk-th banana constructed in stage pp a total of r−1r-1 times, hence letting T′T^{\prime} denote the construction given by omitting the last stage, we obtain 𝕌⁡(T)=𝕃r−1​𝕌​(T′)\mathbb{U}(T)=\mathbb{L}^{r-1}\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime}).

The final case involves the deletion-contraction relation derived in [AM11b, Thm 5.3]. We consider a melonic construction TT of depth n>1n>1 such that tn=((a1,…,ar),p,k)t_{n}=((a_{1},\ldots,a_{r}),p,k) corresponds to adding more than one banana, at least one of which has more than one edge. We denote the resulting graph by GG. Letting 1≤m≤r1\leq m\leq r be such that ama_{m} is the maximum number of edges of the bananas added in stage nn, we may consider the graph G′G^{\prime} giving by replacing the ama_{m}-banana with a 11-banana. Letting ee denote the single edge of the 1−1-banana, G=Gm​e′G=G^{\prime}_{me} is the graph obtained from G′G^{\prime} by replacing ee with mm-parallel edges. Note that as TT is reduced and n>1n>1, ee is neither a bridge nor a looping edge of G′G^{\prime}. Applying the deletion-contraction relation (2.9) then gives

(2.11) 𝕌⁡(Gam​e′)=fam​𝕌​(G′)+gam​𝕌​(G′/e)+ham​𝕌​(G′∖e).\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime}_{a_{m}e})=f_{a_{m}}\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime})+g_{a_{m}}\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime}/e)+h_{a_{m}}\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime}\setminus e).

Rewriting in terms of Grothendieck classes of melonic graphs gives

(2.12) 𝕌⁡(T)=fam​𝕌​(T′)+gam​𝕌​(T′′)+(∏i=1m−1𝔹ai)​(∏i=m+1r𝔹ai)​ham​𝕌​(T′′′)\mathbb{U}(T)=f_{a_{m}}\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime})+g_{a_{m}}\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime\prime})+\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\mathbb{B}_{a_{i}}\right)\left(\prod_{i=m+1}^{r}\mathbb{B}_{a_{i}}\right)h_{a_{m}}\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime\prime\prime})

where T′T^{\prime} is a melonic construction for G′G^{\prime}, T′′T^{\prime\prime} is a melonic construction for G′/eG^{\prime}/e, and T′′′T^{\prime\prime\prime} is a melonic construction obtained from TT be omitting tnt_{n} and decreasing the order of the kkth banana in tpt_{p} by 11. Note that the graph G′∖eG^{\prime}\setminus e corresponds to the melonic graph obtained by taking the melonic graph constructed from T′′′T^{\prime\prime\prime} and attaching two strings of bananas, each at a single vertex.

From this recursive formula for the Grothendieck class, the authors of [AMQ23] proved that for any melonic construction TT, 𝕌⁡(T)\mathbb{U}(T) could be written as a polynomial in 𝕊\mathbb{S} with nonnegative integer coefficients [AMQ23, Cor 3.4]. They also made the following conjecture.

Conjecture 2.3.

Let TT be a melonic construction and 𝕌⁡(T)=a0+a1​𝕊1+…+an​𝕊n\mathbb{U}(T)=a_{0}+a_{1}\mathbb{S}^{1}+\ldots+a_{n}\mathbb{S}^{n} its Grothendieck class. Then, the sequence a0,a1,…,ana_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n} is log-concave.

2.4. Log-concavity and related properties

We briefly recall the definitions of log-concavity and related properties, as well as some key results on the preservation of these properties under certain polynomial operations.

Definition 2.4.

A sequence of nonnegative real numbers a0,…,ana_{0},\ldots,a_{n} is said to

  • •

    be log-concave (LC) if for 0<k<n0<k<n,

    (2.13) ak2≥ak−1​ak+1a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k-1}a_{k+1}
  • •

    be ultra log-concave (ULC) if for 0<k<n0<k<n,

    (2.14) ak2(nk)2≥ak−1(nk−1)​ak+1(nk+1)\frac{a_{k}^{2}}{{n\choose k}^{2}}\geq\frac{a_{k-1}}{{n\choose k-1}}\frac{a_{k+1}}{{n\choose k+1}}

    Note that this condition (2.14) is equivalent to

    (2.15) k⁡(n−k)​ak2≥(n−k+1)​(k+1)​ak−1​ak+1.k(n-k)a_{k}^{2}\geq(n-k+1)(k+1)a_{k-1}a_{k+1}.
  • •

    be unimodal if there exists an index kk such that

    (2.16) a0≤…​ak−1≤ak≥…≥ana_{0}\leq\ldots a_{k-1}\leq a_{k}\geq\ldots\geq a_{n}
  • •

    have no internal zeros if there do not exist indices 0≤i<j<k≤n0\leq i<j<k\leq n such that ai,ak≠0a_{i},a_{k}\neq 0 but aj=0a_{j}=0.

We note that sometimes in the literature, nonnegativity is included in the definition of log-concavity. For the purposes of this paper, we do not take nonnegativity of the aia_{i} to be a necessary condition for log-concavity but do state explicitly when we are considering sequences of nonnegative real numbers specifically.

The above definitions are related to each other in the following ways. First, ultra log-concave is a stronger condition than log-concave. This follows from the observation that the binomial coefficient sequence (n0),…,(nn){n\choose 0},\ldots,{n\choose n} is log-concave. Log-concave sequences are not necessarily unimodal nor have no internal zeros; the sequence 1,0,0,11,0,0,1 is one such example. Positive log-concave sequences are, however, unimodal. Given a sequence of positive real numbers a0,…,ana_{0},\ldots,a_{n} that is log-concave, if there is an index kk such that ak−1≥aka_{k-1}\geq a_{k}, then by log-concavity, ak⋅akak−1≥ak+1a_{k}\cdot\frac{a_{k}}{a_{k-1}}\geq a_{k+1}, hence ak≥ak+1a_{k}\geq a_{k+1}.

In [Lig97], Liggett defines a variation of ultra log-concavity introduced by Pemantle. A sequence of real numbers a0,…,ana_{0},\ldots,a_{n} is said to be ultra log-concave of order mm, shorthand ULC(mm), if ak=0a_{k}=0 for k>mk>m and

(2.17) ak2(mk)2≥ak−1(mk−1)​ak+1(mk+1)\frac{a_{k}^{2}}{{m\choose k}^{2}}\geq\frac{a_{k-1}}{{m\choose k-1}}\frac{a_{k+1}}{{m\choose k+1}}

holds for 0<k<m0<k<m. Once again, this inequality (2.17) is equivalent to

(2.18) k⁡(m−k)​ak2≥(m−k+1)​(k+1)​ak−1​ak+1.k(m-k)a_{k}^{2}\geq(m-k+1)(k+1)a_{k-1}a_{k+1}.

The limiting case, ULC(∞\infty), is given by the condition

(2.19) k​ak2≥(k+1)​ak−1​ak+1ka_{k}^{2}\geq(k+1)a_{k-1}a_{k+1}

for all 0<k<n0<k<n. Note that if a sequence of real numbers if ULC(mm), then it is also ULC(m+1m+1) as n+1n+2>nn+1\frac{n+1}{n+2}>\frac{n}{n+1} for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}.

A polynomial with real coefficients is said to be log-concave, ultra log-concave (of order mm), unimodal, or have no internal zeros if its coefficients form a sequence with the respective property. In [Sta06], Stanley presents a survey of examples of log-concave sequences, properties related to log-concavity, and ways to prove certain real polynomials are log-concave. One such method is given by a result from Newton [Sta06, Thm 2]: if P⁡(x)P(x) is a real polynomial with real zeros, then P⁡(x)P(x) is ultra log-concave.

A key property of (ultra) log-concavity that we use in the following sections is the behavior of (ultra) log-concavity under taking products. More precisely, the statement is as follows.

Proposition 2.5.

Let f⁡(x),g⁡(x)f(x),g(x) be two real polynomials whose coefficients are nonnegative with no internal zeros. Then f⁡(x)​g​(x)f(x)g(x) has no internal zeros and

  1. (1)

    if f⁡(x),g⁡(x)f(x),g(x) are log-concave, then f⁡(x)​g​(x)f(x)g(x) is log-concave.

  2. (2)

    if f⁡(x),g⁡(x)f(x),g(x) are ultra log-concave, then f⁡(x)​g​(x)f(x)g(x) is ultra log-concave.

  3. (3)

    if f⁡(x)f(x) is ULC(nn) and g⁡(x)g(x) is ULC(mm), then f⁡(x)​g​(x)f(x)g(x) is ULC(n+mn+m).

The statement for log-concavity is proved in [Sta06, Prop 2] using linear algebra techniques. A more elementary proof is given in [Koo06, Thm 1]. Liggett proves the statements for ultra log-concavity [Lig97, Thm 2] as a statement for the convolution product of two ultra log-concave sequences that have no internal zeros.

Both log-concavity and ultra log-concavity are also preserved under a shift of the dependent variable.

Proposition 2.6.

Let f⁡(x)f(x) be a real polynomial with nonnegative coefficients and no internal zeros. Then,

  • •

    if f⁡(x)f(x) is log-concave, then f⁡(x+k)f(x+k) is log-concave for any positive integer kk.

  • •

    if f⁡(x)f(x) is ultra-log-concave, then f⁡(x+k)f(x+k) is ultra log-concave for any positive integer kk.

See [Hog74, Thm 2] for the statement on log-concavity. The statement for ultra log-concavity follows from Example 2.26 and Theorem 3.4 of [BH20].

As partial progress towards proving Conjecture 2.3, we start by focusing on what we refer to as the four recursive polynomials involved in the recursive relation (2.12), namely fm​(𝕊),gm​(𝕊),hm​(𝕊),𝔹mf_{m}(\mathbb{S}),g_{m}(\mathbb{S}),h_{m}(\mathbb{S}),\mathbb{B}_{m} for m≥1m\geq 1. (3.6) fm​(s)=(s+1)m−(−1)m(s+1)−(−1)=∑k=0m−1(s+1)k​(−1)m−1−k.f_{m}(s)=\frac{(s+1)^{m}-(-1)^{m}}{(s+1)-(-1)}=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(s+1)^{k}(-1)^{m-1-k}.

3.1. Log-concavity of the recursion polynomials

The goal of this subsection is to prove Theorem 1.1. In what follows, we say a polynomial p⁡(s)=an​sn+…+a0∈ℤ⁡[s]p(s)=a_{n}s^{n}+\ldots+a_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}[s] of degree nn has positive coefficients if ai>0a_{i}>0 for 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n. Note that this is equivalent to the condition that all coefficients are nonnegative, the constant term is positive, and the polynomial has no internal zeroes.

To make use of Proposition 2.5, we first derive a recursive formula for fmf_{m}. For all m≥0m\geq 0, we claim that

(3.10) fm+1​(s)=(s+1)​fm+(−1)m.f_{m+1}(s)=(s+1)f_{m}+(-1)^{m}.

Observe that

fm+1​(s)\displaystyle f_{m+1}(s) =∑k=0m(s+1)k​(−1)m−k=∑k=1m(s+1)k​(−1)m−k+(−1)m\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{m}(s+1)^{k}(-1)^{m-k}=\sum_{k=1}^{m}(s+1)^{k}(-1)^{m-k}+(-1)^{m}
=(s+1)​∑k=0m−1(s+1)k​(−1)m−1−k+(−1)m=(s+1)​fm+(−1)m,\displaystyle=(s+1)\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(s+1)^{k}(-1)^{m-1-k}+(-1)^{m}=(s+1)f_{m}+(-1)^{m},

so indeed (3.10) holds.

Lemma 3.1.

For all m≥1m\geq 1, fmf_{m} is a degree m−1m-1 log-concave polynomial with nonnegative integral coefficients and no internal zeros. More precisely, for m≥2m\geq 2, all coefficients of degree 1≤k≤m−11\leq k\leq m-1 are strictly positive.

Proof.

The statement on the degree of fmf_{m} is clear from (3.6). From (3.10), it is easy to see that the constant term is either 00 or 11 depending on the parity of ff; see also Section 5.1. Similarly, having established nonnegativity of the constant term, by induction using (3.10), the nonconstant coefficients are positive. Note that the positivity condition on the coefficients implies no internal zeroes.

We prove log-concavity by induction on mm. Key to this will be the recursive formula (3.10) together with Proposition 2.5. The first couple cases f1=1,f2=sf_{1}=1,f_{2}=s are all trivially log-concave as monomials. Now, let m≥3m\geq 3 and assume that fm−1f_{m-1} is log-concave with positive nonconstant coefficients. Then, by Proposition 2.5, (s+1)​fm−1(s+1)f_{m-1} is also log-concave with positive nonconstant coefficients. Let aka_{k} denote the degree kk coefficient of fmf_{m}, so ak>0a_{k}>0 for 1≤k≤m−11\leq k\leq m-1 and ak2≥ak+1​ak−1a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k+1}a_{k-1} for 2≤k≤m−12\leq k\leq m-1. It thus suffices to check the log-concavity condition for the degree 11 coefficient of fmf_{m}. The coefficients of fmf_{m} up through degree 4 are computed in terms of mm in Section 5.1. Denoting by aka_{k} the degree kk coefficient, we check that

a12−a0​a2={(m−1)24−(m−1)24=0m​ is oddm24>0m​ is even.a_{1}^{2}-a_{0}a_{2}=\begin{cases}\frac{(m-1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(m-1)^{2}}{4}=0&m\text{ is odd}\\ \frac{m^{2}}{4}>0&m\text{ is even}\end{cases}.

Thus, fmf_{m} is log-concave. ∎

Corollary 3.1.1.

For all m≥1m\geq 1, hmh_{m} is a degree m−1m-1 log-concave polynomial with nonnegative integer coefficients and no internal zeros.

Proof.

As fmf_{m}, (s+1)(s+1) are log-concave with nonnegative integer coefficients and no internal zeros for all mm, by Proposition 2.5, (3.9) tells us that hmh_{m} is also log-concave with nonnegative integer coefficients and no internal zeros for all m≥1m\geq 1. The statement on degree follows from Lemma 3.1 and (3.9). ∎

Lemma 3.2.

For all m≥1m\geq 1, gmg_{m} is a degree m−1m-1 log-concave polynomial with positive integer coefficients.

Proof.

We adapt the method used to prove Lemma 3.1. It is clear that g1=0g_{1}=0 satisfies the statement, so it suffices to consider m≥2m\geq 2. First, for all n≥1,m≥1n\geq 1,m\geq 1, we define

(3.11) gm,n​(s)=n​(s+1)m−1−fm.g_{m,n}(s)=n(s+1)^{m-1}-f_{m}.

Observe that then

(3.12) gm+1,n​(s)=n​(s+1)m−fm+1=(s+1)​gm,n−(−1)m.g_{m+1,n}(s)=n(s+1)^{m}-f_{m+1}=(s+1)g_{m,n}-(-1)^{m}.

Note that for n≥2n\geq 2,

g1,n=n−f1=n−1g2,n=n⁡(s+1)−f2=(n−1)​s+ng_{1,n}=n-f_{1}=n-1\quad\quad g_{2,n}=n(s+1)-f_{2}=(n-1)s+n

are both log-concave with positive integer coefficients. We fix n≥2n\geq 2 and proceed by induction on mm to show that gm,ng_{m,n} is a log-concave polynomial of degree m−1m-1 with positive integer coefficients for all m≥2m\geq 2. The case m=2m=2 is given above. Let m≥3m\geq 3. Assume gm−1,ng_{m-1,n} is a log-concave polynomial of degree m−2m-2 with positive integer coefficients. The product (s+1)​gm−1,n(s+1)g_{m-1,n} is then degree m−1m-1 with positive integer coefficients which are log-concave by Proposition 2.5. From (3.7), the constant term of gm,ng_{m,n} is at least n−1>0n-1>0. It then suffices to check that the degree 11 coefficient of gm,ng_{m,n} satisfies the log-concave inequality, which is done in Section 5.2.

Taking n=mn=m gives the statement for gm=gm,mg_{m}=g_{m,m} for m≥2m\geq 2. ∎

Lemma 3.3.

For all m≥1m\geq 1, bmb_{m} is a degree mm log-concave polynomial with positive integer coefficients.

Proof.

We take a similar approach as for gmg_{m}.

For integers n,m≥1n,m\geq 1, we define

(3.13) bm,n​(s)=n​(s+1)m−1+(s+1)​fmb_{m,n}(s)=n(s+1)^{m-1}+(s+1)f_{m}

Observe that then

(3.14) bm+1,n​(s)=n​(s+1)m+(s+1)​fm+1=(s+1)​bm,n+(−1)m​(s+1)b_{m+1,n}(s)=n(s+1)^{m}+(s+1)f_{m+1}=(s+1)b_{m,n}+(-1)^{m}(s+1)

Note that

b1,n=n+(s+1)​f1=s+n+1b2,n=n⁡(s+1)+(s+1)​f2=s2+(n+1)​s+nb_{1,n}=n+(s+1)f_{1}=s+n+1\quad\quad b_{2,n}=n(s+1)+(s+1)f_{2}=s^{2}+(n+1)s+n

are both log-concave with positive integer coefficients. In fact, as fmf_{m} is degree m−1m-1 with nonnegative integer coefficients by Lemma 3.1, bm,nb_{m,n} is degree mm with positive integer coefficients for all n,m≥1n,m\geq 1.

We prove by induction on mm that bm,nb_{m,n} is log-concave for m,n≥1m,n\geq 1. Let n≥1,m≥3n\geq 1,m\geq 3 and assume that bm−1,nb_{m-1,n} is log-concave. Then, (s+1)​bm−1,n(s+1)b_{m-1,n} is also log-concave, so by (3.14), to show that bm,nb_{m,n} is log-concave, it suffices to check that the degree 2 and degree 1 coefficients both satisfy the log-concave inequality. We do this by explicit computations, given in Section 5.3. We thus see that bm,nb_{m,n} is log-concave, completing the inductive proof. Taking n=mn=m gives the desired result for bm=bm,mb_{m}=b_{m,m}, m≥1m\geq 1. ∎

Altogether, we have the following result.

Theorem 3.4.

For all m≥0m\geq 0, fm,gm,hm,f_{m},g_{m},h_{m}, and bmb_{m} are log-concave with nonnegative integer coefficients and no internal zeros.

Remark 3.5.

Note that the result for banana graphs also establishes the same result for any string of bananas by the multiplicative property of the Grothendieck class of a graph and Proposition 2.5.

For completion, we reprove Corollary 3.4 of [AMQ23].

Corollary 3.5.1.

Let TT be a melonic construction. Suppose the graph obtained from TT has nn edges. We may then write 𝕌⁡(T)=P⁡(𝕊)\mathbb{U}(T)=P(\mathbb{S}) for some degree nn polynomial P⁡(t)∈ℤ⁡[t]P(t)\in\mathbb{Z}[t] with positive coefficients.

Proof.

We first use the recursion described at the end of Section 2.3 to prove that 𝕌⁡(T)\mathbb{U}(T) may be written as a polynomial of degree nn in 𝕊\mathbb{S} with nonnegative integral coefficients. Recall that fm,gm,hmf_{m},g_{m},h_{m} are all of degree m−1m-1 while bmb_{m} is of degree mm. In particular, an mm-banana has a Grothendieck class of degree mm in 𝕊\mathbb{S}. The Grothendieck class of a string of bananas is just the product of the classes of the individual bananas in the string, hence the degree of the class in 𝕊\mathbb{S} is the total number of edges. If TT is a melonic construction whose last stage is ((1,…,1),p,k)((1,\ldots,1),p,k), then 𝕌⁡(T)=(𝕊+2)r−1​𝕌​(T′)\mathbb{U}(T)=(\mathbb{S}+2)^{r-1}\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime}) where rr is the length of the tuple (1,…,1)(1,\ldots,1) and T′T^{\prime} is obtained from TT by omitting the last stage. Assuming that 𝕌⁡(T′)\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime}) is of degree dd where dd is the number of edges of the graph determined by T′T^{\prime}, we then have that GG has d+r−1d+r-1 edges and 𝕌⁡(T)\mathbb{U}(T) is of degree d+r−1d+r-1.

For the final case involving the deletion-contraction relation, use notation as in the end of Section 2.3 and let dd be the number of edges of G′G^{\prime}. Then G′/e,G′∖eG^{\prime}/e,G^{\prime}\setminus e both have d−1d-1 edges and GG has d+am−1d+a_{m}-1 edges. Let G′′′G^{\prime\prime\prime} be the graph determined by T′′′T^{\prime\prime\prime} and let n′n^{\prime} be the total number of edges in the (one or two) strings of bananas whose attachment to vertices in G′′′G^{\prime\prime\prime} give G′∖eG^{\prime}\setminus e. Then G′′′G^{\prime\prime\prime} has d−1−n′d-1-n^{\prime} edges. Assume the Grothendieck classes of T′,T′′,T′′′T^{\prime},T^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime\prime} are of degrees equal to the number of edges of G′,G′′,G′′′G^{\prime},G^{\prime\prime},G^{\prime\prime\prime} respectively. By (2.12), we then have that 𝕌⁡(T)\mathbb{U}(T) is a polynomial given by a sum of polynomials with nonnegative coefficients of degree am−1+d,am−1+d−1,am−1+n′+d−1−n′a_{m}-1+d,a_{m}-1+d-1,a_{m}-1+n^{\prime}+d-1-n^{\prime} respectively, hence 𝕌⁡(T)\mathbb{U}(T) is of degree d+am−1d+a_{m}-1, the number of edges of GG.

We also use the recursion to prove the statement on positivity of the coefficients. First, observe that bmb_{m} has positive coefficients by Lemma 3.3, hence any product ∏i=1rbmi\prod_{i=1}^{r}b_{m_{i}} will also have positive coefficients. This covers the case of a string of bananas. For a melonic graph GG obtained from another G′G^{\prime} by splitting an edge rr times, assuming that 𝕌⁡(G′)\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime}) has positive coefficients, 𝕌⁡(G)=(𝕊+2)r−1​𝕌​(G′)\mathbb{U}(G)=(\mathbb{S}+2)^{r-1}\mathbb{U}(G^{\prime}) also has positive coefficients as this property is preserved under products.

Finally, we consider the case where the last stage of the construction TT is of the form tl=((a1,…,ar),p,k)t_{l}=((a_{1},\ldots,a_{r}),p,k) with am=max⁡{ai}1≤i≤r>1a_{m}=\max\{a_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq r}>1. Observe that while fam,hamf_{a_{m}},h_{a_{m}} may have a zero constant term depending on the parity of ama_{m}, gamg_{a_{m}} has a nonzero constant term for am>1{a_{m}}>1. Assuming 𝕌⁡(T′),𝕌⁡(T′′),𝕌⁡(T′′′)\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime}),\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime\prime}),\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime\prime\prime}) all have positive coefficients, it then follows that gam​𝕌​(T′′)g_{a_{m}}\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime\prime}) has positive coefficients and fam​𝕌​(T′),f_{a_{m}}\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime}), ham​𝕌​(T′′′)​∏i≠mbaih_{a_{m}}\mathbb{U}(T^{\prime\prime\prime})\prod_{i\neq m}b_{a_{i}} both have positive nonconstant coefficients. Thus, 𝕌⁡(T)\mathbb{U}(T) has positive coefficients. ∎

3.2. Ultra log-concavity for the recursion polynomials

A natural question to ask following Theorem 3.4 is if the recursive polynomials satisfy the stronger property of being ultra log-concave.

We first fix some language. Let p⁡(s)∈ℝ⁡[s]p(s)\in\mathbb{R}[s] be an arbitrary polynomial of degree dd. Denote by aja_{j} the coefficient of the degree jj term of pp for 0≤j≤d0\leq j\leq d. We set aj=0a_{j}=0 for integers j>dj>d and j<0j<0. We will say that the coefficient of degree k>0k>0 satisfies the ULC inequality (2.14, 2.15) if k⁡(d−k)​ak2≥(k+1)​(d−k+1)​ak−1​ak+1k(d-k)a_{k}^{2}\geq(k+1)(d-k+1)a_{k-1}a_{k+1}.

We give the results of checking ultra log-concavity for m=1m=1 through m=10m=10 below. The computations were carried out in Sage [Sag]. For the coefficients, the list has indexes corresponding to the degree of the term, i.e. a coefficient list [1,2,3][1,2,3] would correspond to the polynomial 3​s2+2​s+13s^{2}+2s+1.

Lemma 3.6.

Taking gm,ng_{m,n} as defined previously (3.11), for all m,n≥1m,n\geq 1, all coefficients of degree at least 33 satisfy the ULC inequality.

Proof.

Fix n≥1n\geq 1. We denote by gm,n,2g_{m,n,2} the polynomial obtained from gm,ng_{m,n} by omitting the terms of degree 0 and 1. In other words, if a0,a1a_{0},a_{1} are the coefficients of the terms of degree 0,1 in gm,ng_{m,n} respectively, then

gm,n​(s)=gm,n,2​(s)+a1​s+a0.g_{m,n}(s)=g_{m,n,2}(s)+a_{1}s+a_{0}.

The condition that all coefficients of degree at least 33 satisfy the ULC inequality is equivalent to gm,n,2g_{m,n,2} being ultra log-concave. This is trivially true when gm,ng_{m,n} is of degree less than 44, i.e. when m≤4m\leq 4. We proceed by induction. Let m≥5m\geq 5 and assume that gm−1,n,2g_{m-1,n,2} is ultra log-concave. By Proposition 2.5, (s+1)​gm−1,n,2(s+1)g_{m-1,n,2} is then ultra log-concave.

Let a0,a1a_{0},a_{1} denote the coefficients of the degree 0,1 terms of gm−1,ng_{m-1,n} respectively. Observe using (3.12) that then

gm,n​(s)\displaystyle g_{m,n}(s) =(s+1)​gm−1,n,2+(s+1)​(a1​s+a0)−(−1)m−1\displaystyle=(s+1)g_{m-1,n,2}+(s+1)(a_{1}s+a_{0})-(-1)^{m-1}
=(s+1)​gm−1,n,2+a1​s2+(a1+a0)​s+a0−(−1)m−1,\displaystyle=(s+1)g_{m-1,n,2}+a_{1}s^{2}+(a_{1}+a_{0})s+a_{0}-(-1)^{m-1},

so

gm,n,2​(s)=(s+1)​gm−1,n,2+a1​s2.g_{m,n,2}(s)=(s+1)g_{m-1,n,2}+a_{1}s^{2}.

It then suffices to check that the degree 3 coefficient of gm,ng_{m,n} satisfies the ULC inequality. This is done in Section 5.2. ∎

Lemma 3.7.

Taking bm,nb_{m,n} as defined previously (3.13), for all m≥1,n≥3m\geq 1,n\geq 3, all coefficients of degree at least 33 satisfy the ULC inequality.

Proof.

Fix n≥2n\geq 2. As in Lemma 3.6, we denote by bm,n,2b_{m,n,2} the polynomial obtained from bm,nb_{m,n} by omitting the terms of degree 0 and 1. The condition that all coefficients of degree at least 33 satisfy the ULC inequality is then equivalent to bm,n,2b_{m,n,2} being ultra log-concave. By Proposition 2.5, (s+1)​bm−1,n,2(s+1)b_{m-1,n,2} is then ultra log-concave. Let a0,a1a_{0},a_{1} denote the coefficients of the degree 0,1 terms of bm−1,nb_{m-1,n} respectively. bm,n​(s)\displaystyle b_{m,n}(s) =(s+1)​bm−1,n,2+(s+1)​(a1​s+a0)+(−1)m−1​(s+1)\displaystyle=(s+1)b_{m-1,n,2}+(s+1)(a_{1}s+a_{0})+(-1)^{m-1}(s+1)
=(s+1)​bm−1,n,2+a1​s2+(a1+a0+(−1)m−1)​s+a0+(−1)m−1,\displaystyle=(s+1)b_{m-1,n,2}+a_{1}s^{2}+(a_{1}+a_{0}+(-1)^{m-1})s+a_{0}+(-1)^{m-1},

bm,n,2​(s)=(s+1)​bm−1,n,2+a1​s2.b_{m,n,2}(s)=(s+1)b_{m-1,n,2}+a_{1}s^{2}.

It then suffices to check that the degree 3 coefficient of bm,nb_{m,n} satisfies the ULC inequality. This is done in Section 5.3. Note that the assumption that n≥3n\geq 3 rather than n≥1n\geq 1 or n≥2n\geq 2 is necessary here as the statement is false for m=6,n=1m=6,n=1 and m=4,n=2m=4,n=2. ∎

Proposition 3.8.

(ultra log-concavity of fm,gm,hm,bmf_{m},g_{m},h_{m},b_{m})

For m≥4m\geq 4, fm,gm,hm,f_{m},g_{m},h_{m}, and bmb_{m} have the following properties.

When mm is odd:

  • •

    fmf_{m} is not ultra log-concave and the coefficients of degree 1 and 3 fail the ULC inequality while the coefficient of degree 2 satisfies the ULC inequality.

  • •

    gmg_{m} is not ultra log-concave and the only coefficient that fails the ULC inequality is degree 2.

  • •

    hmh_{m} is not ultra log-concave and the coefficient of degree 3 fails the ULC inequality while the coefficient of degrees 1 and 2 satisfy the ULC inequality.

  • •

    bmb_{m} is not ultra log-concave and the only coefficient that fails the ULC inequality is degree 1.

When mm is even:

  • •

    fmf_{m} is not ultra log-concave and the coefficient of degree 2 fails the ULC inequality while the coefficients of degrees 1 and 3 satisfy the ULC inequality.

  • •

    gmg_{m} is not ultra log-concave and the only coefficient that fails the ULC inequality is degree 1.

  • •

    hmh_{m} is not ultra log-concave and the coeficients of degrees 1 and 2 fail the ULC inequality while the coefficient of degree 2 satisfies the ULC inequality

  • •

    bmb_{m} is ultra log-concave

Proof.

The statements for gm,bmg_{m},b_{m} are given by taking n=mn=m in Lemmas 3.6,3.7 and checking the ULC inequality for the coefficients of degrees 1 and 2, which is done in Sections 5.2 and 5.3. The statements for fmf_{m} may be checked by explicit computation, as in Section 5.1. For hmh_{m}, observe using equations (3.9) and (3.10) that

(3.15) hm​(s)=fm​(s)+(−1)m.h_{m}(s)=f_{m}(s)+(-1)^{m}.

Then, the only coefficient of hmh_{m} that differs from fmf_{m} is the degree 0 coefficient. It then suffices to check whether or not the degree 1 coefficient satisfies the ULC inequality. Let aja_{j} denote the coefficient of the degree jj term of hmh_{m}. For mm odd, a0=0a_{0}=0, so the ULC inequality is satisfied. For m≥4m\geq 4 even, a0=1a_{0}=1, so using the coefficients of fmf_{m} calculated in Section 5.1, we have

(m−2)​a12−2​(m−1)​a0​a2=m⁡(m−2)2−m​(m−2)​(m−1)2=−m​(m−2)22<0,(m-2)a_{1}^{2}-2(m-1)a_{0}a_{2}=\frac{m(m-2)}{2}-\frac{m(m-2)(m-1)}{2}=-\frac{m(m-2)^{2}}{2}<0,

hence the degree 1 coefficient fails the ULC inequality. ∎

Computer computations for m=1m=1 through m=100m=100 suggest the following.

Conjecture 3.9.

For m≥4m\geq 4, both fmf_{m} and hmh_{m} are not ultra log-concave and all coefficients of degree 4≤j≤m−24\leq j\leq m-2 fail the ULC inequality.

3.3. Ultra-log-concavity of order mm for the recursion polynomials

The polynomials fm,gm,hmf_{m},g_{m},h_{m} are slightly better behaved with respect to being ultra log-concave of order mm (rather than m−1m-1). Note that bmb_{m} is of degree mm, hence the results for the ultra log-concavity of order mm for bmb_{m} are covered by Proposition 3.8, though we include them again in Proposition 3.10 for completeness. As before, let p⁡(s)∈ℝ⁡[s]p(s)\in\mathbb{R}[s] be a polynomial of degree d<md<m and denote by aja_{j} the coefficient of the degree jj term of pp for 0≤j≤d0\leq j\leq d with aj=0a_{j}=0 for j>dj>d. We say that the coefficient of degree k>0k>0 satisfies the ULC(mm) inequality (2.18) if k⁡(m−k)​ak2≥(k+1)​(m−k+1)​ak−1​ak+1k(m-k)a_{k}^{2}\geq(k+1)(m-k+1)a_{k-1}a_{k+1}.

We first give the results of ULC(mm) for fm,gm,hmf_{m},g_{m},h_{m} computed for m=1m=1 through m=10m=10 below. As before, the coefficients are listed in order [a0,…,am−1][a_{0},\ldots,a_{m-1}].

Proposition 3.10.

(ultra log-concavity of order mm of fm,gm,hm,bmf_{m},g_{m},h_{m},b_{m})

For m≥6m\geq 6, fm,gm,hm,f_{m},g_{m},h_{m}, and bmb_{m} have the following properties.

When mm is odd:

  • •

    fmf_{m} is not ULC(mm) and the only coefficient that fails the ULC(mm) inequality is degree 11.

  • •

    gmg_{m} is ULC(mm).

  • •

    hmh_{m} is ULC(mm).

  • •

    bmb_{m} is not ULC(mm) and the only coefficient that fails the ULC(mm) inequality is degree 1.

When mm is even:

  • •

    fmf_{m} is not ULC(mm) and the only coefficient that fails the ULC(mm) inequality is degree 22.

  • •

    gmg_{m} is not ULC(mm) and the only coefficient that fails the ULC(mm) inequality is degree 11.

  • •

    hmh_{m} is not ULC(mm) and the only coefficients that fail the ULC(mm) inequality are degrees 1,21,2.

  • •

    bmb_{m} is ULC(mm).

Proof.

We first prove by induction on mm that for all m≥0m\geq 0, all coefficients of degree at least 3 satisfy the ULC(mm) inequality for fmf_{m}. As before, we denote by fm,2f_{m,2} the polynomial obtained from fmf_{m} by omitting the terms of degree 0 and 1. The condition that all coefficients of degree at least 3 satisfy the ULC(mm) inequality for fmf_{m} is equivalent to fm,2f_{m,2} being ULC(mm). Let a0,a1a_{0},a_{1} be the coefficients of the terms of degree 0, 1 in fmf_{m}. Then, using (3.10),

fm+1​(s)=(s+1)​fm,2+(s+1)​(a1​s+a0)+(−1)m=(s+1)​fm,2+a1​s2+(a0+a1)​s+a0+(−1)m,f_{m+1}(s)=(s+1)f_{m,2}+(s+1)(a_{1}s+a_{0})+(-1)^{m}=(s+1)f_{m,2}+a_{1}s^{2}+(a_{0}+a_{1})s+a_{0}+(-1)^{m},

so

fm+1,2=(s+1)​fm,2+a1​s2.f_{m+1,2}=(s+1)f_{m,2}+a_{1}s^{2}.

For 0≤m≤40\leq m\leq 4, fmf_{m} is of degree at most 33, hence fm,2f_{m,2} is trivially ULC(mm). Let m≥5m\geq 5 and assume that fm−1,2f_{m-1,2} is ULC(m−1m-1). By Proposition 2.5, (s+1)​fm,2(s+1)f_{m,2} is then ULC(mm). It then suffices to check that the degree 3 coefficients of fmf_{m} satisfies the ULC(mm). This is done explicitly in Section 5.1. The checking of the statements about the degree 1 and 2 coefficients of fmf_{m} may also be found in Section 5.1.

As before, by (3.15), the statements for hmh_{m} follow from that of fmf_{m} and checking ULC(mm) inequality for the degree 1 coefficient of hmh_{m}, as below:

m​ odd:(m−1)​a12−2​m​a0​a2=(m−1)34>0m\text{ odd}:\quad(m-1)a_{1}^{2}-2ma_{0}a_{2}=\frac{(m-1)^{3}}{4}>0
m​ even:(m−1)​a12−2​m​a0​a2=m2​(m−1)4−m2​(m−2)2=−m2​(m−3)4<0m\text{ even}:\quad(m-1)a_{1}^{2}-2ma_{0}a_{2}=\frac{m^{2}(m-1)}{4}-\frac{m^{2}(m-2)}{2}=-\frac{m^{2}(m-3)}{4}<0

Finally, the statements for gmg_{m} and bmb_{m} follow from the previous proposition. More precisely, as ULC(m−1m-1) implies ULC(mm), by Proposition 3.8, all coefficients of degree at least 3 of gmg_{m} satisfy the ULC(mm) inequality. It then suffices to check the degree 1 and 2 coefficients, which is done in Section 5.2. ∎

4. Necklace Graphs

In this section, we take necklace graphs to be graphs obtained by multiplying the edges of a polygon. Equivalently, a necklace graph is obtained from a string of bananas by identifying the two outer endpoints. This section is inspired by Remark 2.2 of [AMQ23] where the authors introduce the necklace graph consisting of only 22-bananas, which we discuss shortly. The main result of this section is log-concavity of the Grothendieck classes of a specific infinite subfamily of necklace graphs, which we call clasped necklaces, described below.

4.1. Necklace graph of 22-bananas

In Remark 2.2 of [AMQ23], the authors introduce the necklace graph consisting of only 22-bananas. A corresponding melonic construction for the necklace graph of nn 22-bananas is (((3),0,1),((2,…,2),1,1))(((3),0,1),((2,\ldots,2),1,1)) where the tuple (2,…,2)(2,\ldots,2) has length n−1n-1. More generally, for m≥1,n≥2m\geq 1,n\geq 2, we denote by Gm,nG_{m,n} the necklace graph of nn mm-bananas with melonic construction given by (((m+1),0,1),((m,…,m),1,1))(((m+1),0,1),((m,\ldots,m),1,1)) where (m,…,m)(m,\ldots,m) has length n−1n-1. We take Gm,1G_{m,1} to be the graph with one vertex and mm-loops. Note that Gm,2G_{m,2} is just a 2​m2m-banana. Observe that for n≥3n\geq 3, G1,nG_{1,n} is an nn-sided polygon, hence may be obtained from a 22-banana by splitting an edge n−2n-2 times. Its Grothendieck class is then

(4.1) 𝕌⁡(G1,n)=𝔹2​(𝕊+2)n−2\mathbb{U}(G_{1,n})=\mathbb{B}_{2}(\mathbb{S}+2)^{n-2}

which is ultra log-concave in 𝕊\mathbb{S} by Proposition 2.5 as 𝔹2\mathbb{B}_{2} is ultra log-concave in 𝕊\mathbb{S}.

The necklace graph of nn 22-bananas, G2,nG_{2,n}, has Grothendieck class

(4.2) 𝕌⁡(G2,n)=(𝕋n+n​𝕋n−1−1)​(𝕋+1)n−1​𝕋=((𝕊+1)n+n​(𝕊+1)n−1−1)​(𝕊+2)n−1​(𝕊+1)\mathbb{U}(G_{2,n})=(\mathbb{T}^{n}+n\mathbb{T}^{n-1}-1)(\mathbb{T}+1)^{n-1}\mathbb{T}=((\mathbb{S}+1)^{n}+n(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n-1}-1)(\mathbb{S}+2)^{n-1}(\mathbb{S}+1)

as given in [AMQ23, Remark 6.3]. This formula may be proved by induction using (4.3) and (4.6) below. By observing that

(𝕊+1)n+n​(𝕊+1)n−1−1=(𝕊+1)n−1​(𝕊+1+n)−1,(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n}+n(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n-1}-1=(\mathbb{S}+1)^{n-1}(\mathbb{S}+1+n)-1,

we see that 𝕌⁡(G2,n)\mathbb{U}(G_{2,n}) is also ultra log-concave in 𝕊\mathbb{S}.

4.2. Clasped necklaces

For m≥1,n≥2m\geq 1,n\geq 2, define the clasped necklace Gm,n′G_{m,n}^{\prime} to be the necklace graph of n−1n-1 mm-bananas and a single 11-banana. The clasped necklace G3,7′G^{\prime}_{3,7} is pictured in Figure 2 below. The graph has melonic construction ((m+1,0,1),((1,m,…,m),1,1))((m+1,0,1),((1,m,\ldots,m),1,1)) where (1,m,…,m)(1,m,\ldots,m) has length n−1n-1. Note that for n≥3n\geq 3, Gm,n′/e=Gm,n−1G_{m,n}^{\prime}/e=G_{m,n-1} and Gm,n′∖eG_{m,n}^{\prime}\setminus e is a string of n−1n-1 mm-bananas. The deletion-contraction relation then gives

(4.3) 𝕌⁡(Gm,n)=fm​𝕌​(Gm,n′)+gm​𝕌​(Gm,n−1)+hm​𝔹mn−1.\mathbb{U}(G_{m,n})=f_{m}\mathbb{U}(G_{m,n}^{\prime})+g_{m}\mathbb{U}(G_{m,n-1})+h_{m}\mathbb{B}_{m}^{n-1}.

Let Gm,n′′G_{m,n}^{\prime\prime} be the graph obtained from Gm,n−1′G^{\prime}_{m,n-1} by splitting the edge ee, so Gm,n′′G_{m,n}^{\prime\prime} is the necklace graph of 22 11-bananas and n−2n-2 mm-bananas. Then, Gm,n′=(Gm,n′′)m​e′G_{m,n}^{\prime}=(G_{m,n}^{\prime\prime})_{me^{\prime}} where e′e^{\prime} is an edge added from the splitting of ee. Observe that then Gm,n′′/e′=Gm,n−1′G_{m,n}^{\prime\prime}/e^{\prime}=G_{m,n-1}^{\prime} and Gm,n′′∖e′G_{m,n}^{\prime\prime}\setminus e^{\prime} is a string of n−2n-2 mm bananas and a single 11-banana. It follows that

Proposition 4.2 (Log-concavity for clasped necklaces).

For m≥1,n≥2m\geq 1,n\geq 2, the class of the clasped necklace graph of n−1n-1 mm bananas and a single 11-banana is log-concave in 𝕊\mathbb{S}.

The open source mathematics software Sage ([Sag]) was used to simplify some algebraic expressions. As the computations are straightforward, we state only the resulting simplified expressions. Throughout the following, unless otherwise stated, aia_{i} denotes the coefficient of the degree ii term of the polynomial in question. It is assumed in the expression for aja_{j} that the polynomial has degree at least jj (aj=0a_{j}=0 otherwise). Further, when checking either the log-concave (LC) inequality (2.13) or the ultra log-concave (ULC) inequality (2.15) for degree jj, we may assume that the polynomial has degree at least j+1j+1 as otherwise the inequalities are both trivially satisfied by aj+1=0a_{j+1}=0. Note that for m≥1m\geq 1, fm,gm,n,hmf_{m},g_{m,n},h_{m} are all of degree m−1m-1 while bm,nb_{m,n} is of degree mm.
